blocks.text: A derivative is a financial contract whose value is derived from an underlying asset. In currency derivatives, the underlying asset is the exchange rate between two currencies (e.g., USD/INR).
A forward contract is an agreement to buy or sell a currency at a future date at a price decided today. These are traded in the Over-the-Counter (OTC) market.

items: Customized: Tailor-made for specific amounts and dates.
Counterparty Risk: High risk of default as there is no exchange guarantee.
Settlement: Usually settled by physical delivery at the end of the contract.

blocks.text: Currency Futures are standardized contracts traded on an exchange (like NSE or BSE) to buy or sell currency at a future date.
Key Difference: Unlike Forwards, Futures are standardized (fixed lot sizes/dates), have zero counterparty risk (guaranteed by the Clearing Corporation), and are marked-to-market daily.
Options give the buyer the RIGHT but not the OBLIGATION to buy or sell currency at a specific price.

items: Premium: The price paid by the buyer to the seller to acquire this right.

blocks.text: Pricing of currency futures is primarily based on Interest Rate Parity. It states that the difference between the forward rate and spot rate depends on the interest rate differential between the two countries.
Formula Concept: If Indian interest rates are higher than US rates, the USD/INR Future price is generally higher than the Spot price (Premium).
